content.comment_body: Hello, I hope the image I attached clarifies my issue. I have two [product_name] devices: one basic and one pure variant, at IPs 192.168.0.2 and 192.168.0.3. I don't have three devices as shown in the online diagram. I'd like to remove the 'unknown' device. Thanks!

I've attached a video of the online view. The [product_name] with IP 192.168.178.31 is a pure model running [version_no].0. As you can see, the issue still exists when this device is not powered on. I'm not sure if the difference between your device ([version_no].2) and mine ([version_no].0) is the cause. If I were you, I would consider starting a support request.

I had previously entered an [article_no] ([article_no]) instead of what it actually was – [article_no]. After correcting this, everything works properly now. Thanks for the reply and video, [user_name]. It pointed me in the right direction. Quick question: Where does the FS4 label come from? These part numbers are quite mysterious to me. Thanks!

This isn't just confusing for you. Since the latest [product_name], [company_name] updated the order number system. The numbering now has three segments, separated by hyphens. Previously, up to [version_no].1 (the first FS4-[product_name]), the device series spec was in the last segment, for example [article_no] for that model. When [article_no] appeared, adding another series ([article_no]) became tricky since only 4 digits fit there. So, when [version_no].2 arrived, the series identifier was moved to the middle segment, and the last segment became [article_no]. This approach allows further extension of device series numbers in the future.

Thanks, [user_name], your post helped clarify the recent changes in [product_name] part numbers. Now I understand the pattern and where my network configuration went wrong. It used to make sense that the last digit of the part number identified the version, but the change confused me. Another question—does 'FS4' reference firmware? I'm confused as it's not labeled on the device. Will future releases increase both the middle segment and FS (e.g., FS5, FS6)? For context, I started using these devices back when automating greenhouses in Virginia in the 90s, even collaborating with [company_name] Greenhouse Automation. Back then we worked with [version_no], [version_no], and C7 controllers. I remember a sales representative introducing the first version of [product_name] to me—it was new and unfamiliar. Over a weekend, I explored its logic functions and found it very simple to use. Later, I used many of the 'Long' variants in my network setups. Compared to other programming environments, it was much easier. Over time, I implemented these controllers widely for simple tasks, and they worked great! Now, after 25 years, it's amazing to see how much [product_name] has improved. Thanks to the dedicated development team for making this product better year after year! I'm a long-time fan.

Hi [user_name], it's true—the recent changes in firmware versions and order numbers are challenging to follow, and you're not alone in feeling lost. From my previous attachment, you can see several [product_name] devices with different firmware versions (FS). For instance: [version_no].0 devices include firmware versions FS01, FS02, and FS03, often shown as [article_no] in hardware selection. [version_no].1 devices have FS04, FS05, and FS06 and display as [product_name].FS4; these can be updated. Frankly, I think these should have started as a new series ([article_no]) and reset firmware labeling. [version_no].2 models have FS01 and FS02 and also show as [product_name].FS4, so ideally this should have been [article_no]. Firmware started over at FS01, but selection labeling hasn't changed, and firmware updates between [version_no].1 and [version_no].2 don't work. As for your question, yes, FS4 is related to firmware—the first [article_no]-[product_name] devices with FS04 got that identifier in hardware selection. Unfortunately, the logic behind the system isn’t clear to me.

analysis.insight_summary: Users in this thread discuss confusion and difficulties configuring [company_name] networked controllers due to unclear device and part number labeling. The primary experience issues are changes in device nomenclature, firmware, and order numbering, which lack transparency and documentation. This led to users misidentifying hardware in software, causing extra devices to appear in network views. Ongoing changes in numbering conventions and insufficient guidance are significant sources of frustration.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect network views to accurately reflect only connected hardware and want clear, consistent mapping between configured software devices and physical units. Further, they seek straightforward, transparent product and firmware version labeling so that device identity and configuration can be easily understood and tracked.
